candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the multipart/form-data request body, boundary, and each part's headers. By omitting a usable Content-Disposition form-data name, the part is not returned as a FileItem, while its header and body are still parsed and discarded by the multipart iterator.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The per-part header cap in MultipartStream.readHeaders() prevents one enormous part header, but repeated tiny headers are unaffected. Named parts are counted correctly by FileUploadBase, and an application-configured finite maxRequestSize can cap total bytes, but Tomcat's default multipart maxRequestSize is -1 and maxPartCount is documented as the total-part safeguard. The limit is not checked inside the iterator, and no other total-part counter was found in the indexed multipart classes.
candidates.impact: An unauthenticated client can send a long-lived multipart request containing a very large number of tiny unnamed parts. The server continues parsing headers and discarding bodies, consuming network, CPU, and a request-processing thread while the configured maxPartCount never rejects the request. Multiple connections can exhaust worker capacity and deny service to legitimate users.
candidates.prerequisites: A deployed servlet must invoke multipart parsing via getParts(), getPart(), or getParameter() (or casual multipart parsing must be enabled). The application's multipart maxRequestSize must be unset/relaxed enough not to provide an independent bound; the default MultipartConfigElement maxRequestSize is -1.
candidates.root_cause: Tomcat maps maxPartCount to FileUploadBase.fileCountMax, which is checked only against accepted FileItems in parseRequest(). FileItemIteratorImpl.hasNext()/findNextItem() first scans and silently discards any multipart part lacking a usable form-data field name, looping without any total-part counter. Consequently, unnamed or non-form-data parts are never reflected in items.size() and never consume the configured part budget.
candidates.title: Multipart maxPartCount bypass via unnamed parts permits resource-exhaustion DoS
candidates.trace: Connector default maxPartCount is 10 (Connector.java 215). Request.parseParts() sets FileUpload.fileCountMax to the lower of the parameter/part limits (Request.java 2636-2646). FileUploadBase.parseRequest() checks items.size() only after iter.hasNext() has already searched for the next accepted item (FileUploadBase.java 456-460). FileItemIteratorImpl.findNextItem() loops over parts, and for a part with no form-data field name it calls multi.discardBodyData() and continues (FileItemIteratorImpl.java 244-282). The constructor itself calls findNextItem(), so an all-unnamed body can loop indefinitely before parseRequest() ever performs the file-count check. maxPartHeaderSize bounds each individual header to 512 bytes, but does not bound the number of such parts.
candidates.unverified: No runtime test or exploit request was executed. The exact DoS severity depends on whether the target application parses multipart requests and whether it configures a finite maxRequestSize or other reverse-proxy limits. The P1 relation index provides no control/data-flow proof; the trace was verified directly in source text.
candidates.weakness_type: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling (CWE-770)

coverage_summary: Source scope reports 3,031 visible files with no binary/symlink/sensitive-name exclusions. The P1 relation index covers 2,935 files (96 missing from the index), contains syntax-level symbols/calls/containment only, and explicitly provides no control flow, data flow, semantic resolution, or exploitability proof. I reviewed the multipart path end-to-end, plus representative connector/HTTP, authenticator, rewrite, default/WebDAV servlet, web-resource, HTTP/2/HPACK, security-valve/filter, and session-handling code. No build or tests were run, and no runtime behavior was confirmed.
limitations: Static source review only; no code, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were executed.
P1 capabilities omit control/data flow and semantic resolution, and 96 source files are missing from the relation index; unreported areas were not treated as reviewed.
The multipart DoS requires a deployment endpoint that parses multipart bodies and lacks a tighter application/proxy size limit; this deployment context is not present or verified.
The repository snapshot contains no runnable application-specific evidence establishing endpoint reachability or actual worker-exhaustion impact.

rejected_leads.lead: ParameterLimitValve selects the first matching regex while iterating a ConcurrentHashMap, so overlapping broad and specific URL patterns may apply limits non-deterministically.
rejected_leads.reason: The patterns come from trusted administrator/application configuration, and only a path-specific limit bypass or policy inconsistency is evident; this is weaker than the multipart resource-exhaustion path.

rejected_leads.lead: HpackDecoder.getRealIndex() can wrap an out-of-range dynamic table index to zero and handleIndex() lacks the bounds check used by handleIndexedHeaderName(), possibly causing an NPE.
rejected_leads.reason: Source inspection suggests malformed HTTP/2 input could reach an unchecked lookup, but the exception appears connection-local and is caught by the upgrade handler's Throwable handling; no broad security impact was established.

rejected_leads.lead: AbstractStreamProvider falls back to trust-all TrustManagers when no CA certificate is configured.
rejected_leads.reason: This is an explicit warning/fallback for an administrator-configured cloud membership connection and requires that insecure configuration; no default remote exposure or stronger source-supported exploit path was found.

summary: Reviewed the Tomcat 10.1.x source snapshot with emphasis on request parsing, multipart handling, authentication/rewrite paths, servlet resource writes, HTTP/2, and security valves/filters. The strongest source-supported issue is a multipart part-count bypass: Tomcat's new maxPartCount contract is implemented through FileUpload's item-count limit, but the iterator discards unnamed parts before that count is applied, so an attacker can stream an unlimited number of tiny malformed parts. No runtime tests or data-flow analysis were available; this is a lead, not a confirmed exploit.
